questions.question: Two outside addresses tried to guess passwords. Which one eventually got in?
questions.hint: Filter for Accepted. Which logins came from outside the 10.x internal network?
questions.explain: 198.51.100.7 is background noise: a scanner trying default usernames like pi and ftpuser, then giving up. 203.0.113.45 kept going until a login was accepted.

questions.question: Which account did the attacker break into?
questions.hint: Look at the user named in the attacker's Accepted line.
questions.explain: Usernames like admin and test don't exist here (Invalid user), and root was blocked. deploy is a real account with a guessable password: a classic weak spot.

questions.question: At what time did the attacker first log in successfully? (HH:MM:SS)
questions.hint: The timestamp at the start of the first Accepted line from 203.0.113.45.
questions.explain: 03:14:07 is the start of the compromise. In a real case, everything this account did after that moment is suspect.

questions.question: What backdoor account did they create?
questions.explain: sysupd is named to look like a system service. They also added it to the sudo group, and 25 minutes later it logged in from the same attacker address.

questions.question: Which file did they write to so they could log in as root later? (full path)
questions.hint: Filter for sudo and read each COMMAND=. One of them appends to a file with tee -a.
questions.explain: Adding a public key to root's authorized_keys lets the attacker log in as root without any password. Changing deploy's password alone wouldn't lock them out: you'd also need to remove the key and the sysupd account.

cases.title: Uploads gone wrong
cases.intro: shop.example is a small online shop. Customers reported the site felt slow this morning. Read the web server's access log and work out what happened.

questions.question: Which IP address is attacking the shop?
questions.hint: Filter for 404. Normal customers rarely ask for pages that don't exist.
questions.explain: A burst of requests for admin panels, .git and backup files in under two seconds is automated scanning, all from one address.

questions.question: Which scanning tool does its user agent give away?
questions.hint: The user agent is the last quoted part of each line.
questions.explain: Nikto is a free web vulnerability scanner that announces itself by default. Real attackers often change the user agent, so never rely on it alone, but it's a great first clue.

questions.question: Through path traversal, which system file did they successfully read? (full path)
questions.hint: ..%2F is a URL-encoded ../ (step up one folder). Look for traversal requests that returned 200, then decode the path.
questions.explain: download.php trusted the file name it was given, so ../../../../etc/passwd climbed out of the downloads folder. /etc/shadow got a 403, but settings.ini (with the admin password) leaked too.

questions.question: What is the file name of the web shell they uploaded?
questions.hint: Filter for POST, then look for a file in /uploads that's being called with a cmd= parameter.
questions.explain: An upload form accepted a .php file and saved it where the web server runs PHP. Every ?cmd= request after that runs a command on the server.

questions.question: What was the first command they ran through the web shell?
questions.hint: Filter for cmd= and take the earliest one.
questions.explain: id shows which user the web server runs as: the attacker's first question on any new foothold. Later they downloaded something called miner to /tmp/.m and ran it in the background, which explains why the shop felt slow.
